questions.question_text: Dementia of the Alzheimer’s type accounts for what percentages of old age dementias?
questions.explanation: Dementia of the Alzheimer’s type accounts for about 60 percent of old-age dementias[cite: 16]. It is estimated to affect from 5 to 10 percent of people of age 65 years and accounts for the most striking increase in dementia incidence in very old individuals[cite: 16]. Dementia of the Alzheimer’s type and related dementias cost society an estimated $100 billion each year, which includes both direct costs (i.e., actual dollar expenditures) and indirect costs (i.e., resource losses not involving dollar expenditures)[cite: 16]. The greatest risk factor for developing dementia is age[cite: 16]. The incidence and prevalence of the disease double every 5 years after age 60 years[cite: 16]. An estimated 4 million U.S. citizens have Alzheimer’s disease[cite: 16]. As the Baby Boom generation (born in the 1950s and 1960s) moves into the age group of 60 years and older, Alzheimer’s disease will become an even greater public health problem[cite: 16]. The number of Americans Alzheimer’s disease is expected to triple by mid-century, growing from 4.5 million to more than 13 million[cite: 16].

questions.explanation: Although epidemiological studies show that anxiety disorders are less prevalent in older adults compared with younger adults, the prevalence of anxiety disorders in this older age group is high compared with that of other disorders[cite: 16]. Indeed, anxiety disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric disorders, excluding the dementias, in people older than age 65 years[cite: 16]. The most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults is phobic disorder[cite: 16]. Panic disorder is the least common anxiety disorder in this age group[cite: 16]. Across all age groups, anxiety disorders are more prevalent in women than in men[cite: 16]. The prevalence of anxiety disorders decreases with increasing age[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the biology of aging is false?

options.text: The T-cell response to antigens is altered.
Each cell of the body has a genetically determined replicative capacity.

questions.explanation:
As a person ages, the optic lens thickens (not thins) in association with an inability to accommodate (presbyopia), and hearing loss is progressive, particularly at the high frequencies[cite: 16]. The process of aging, known as senescence, results from a complex interaction of genetic, metabolic, hormonal, immunological, and structural factors acting on molecular, cellular, histological, and organ levels[cite: 16]. The most commonly held theory is that each cell of the body has a genetically determined life span during which replication occurs a limited number of times before the cell dies[cite: 16]. One study found 50 such replications in human cells[cite: 16]. Structural changes in cells take place with age[cite: 16]. In the central nervous system (CNS), for example, age-related cell changes occur in neurons, which show signs of degeneration[cite: 16].
A progressive decline in many bodily functions includes a decrease in melanin and decreases in cardiac output and stroke volume, glomerular filtration rate, oxygen consumption, cerebral blood flow, and vital capacity[cite: 16]. Many immune mechanisms are altered, with impaired T-cell response to antigens and an increase in the formation of autoimmune antibodies[cite: 16]. These altered immune responses probably play a role in aged persons’ susceptibility to infection and possibly even to neoplastic disease[cite: 16]. Some neoplasms, most notably cancers of the colon, prostate, stomach, and skin, show a steadily increasing incidence with age[cite: 16].
Variable changes in endocrine function are seen[cite: 16]. For example, postmenopausal estrogen levels decrease, producing breast tissue involution and vaginal epithelial atrophy[cite: 16]. Testosterone levels begin to decline in the sixth decade of life; however, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone increase[cite: 16]. In the CNS, there is a decrease in brain weight, ventricular enlargement, and neuronal loss of approximately 50,000 a day, with some reduction in cerebral blood flow and oxygenation[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about learning and memory in the elderly is false?

options.text: IQ remains stable until age 80 years.
Complete learning of new material still occurs.
On multiple-choice tests, recognition of correct answers persists.

questions.explanation: In elderly persons, simple recall becomes difficult (does not remain intact), and memory-encoding ability diminishes[cite: 16]. These functions decline with age[cite: 16]. However, many cognitive abilities are retained in old age[cite: 16]. Although elderly persons take longer than young persons to learn new material, complete learning of new material still occurs[cite: 16]. Old adults maintain their verbal abilities, and their IQs remain stable until approximately age 80 years[cite: 16]. On multiple-choice tests, recognition of correct answers persists[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: In the physical assessment of elderly adults, which of the following statements is false?

options.text: Toxins of bacterial origin are common.
Cerebral anoxia often precipitates mental syndromes.
Nutritional deficiencies may cause mental symptoms.
The most common metabolic intoxication causing mental symptoms is uremia.

questions.explanation:
Severe vitamin deficiencies in elderly adults are rare (rather than common)[cite: 16]. However, a number of conditions and deficiencies are typical and should be considered in the physical assessment of elderly patients[cite: 16]. Toxins of bacterial origin and metabolic origin are common in old age[cite: 16]. Bacterial toxins usually originate in occult or inconspicuous foci of infection, such as suspected pneumonic conditions and urinary infections[cite: 16]. In elderly individuals, the most common metabolic intoxication causing mental symptoms is uremia, which is an excess of urea and other nitrogenous waste products in the blood[cite: 16]. Mild diabetes, hepatic failure, and gout are also known to cause mental symptoms in elderly people and may easily be missed unless they are actively investigated[cite: 16]. Alcohol and drug misuse may cause many mental disturbances in late life[cite: 16]. These abuses, with their characteristic effects, are usually determined by taking a history[cite: 16].
Cerebral anoxia often precipitates mental symptoms as a result of cardiac insufficiency or emphysema[cite: 16]. Anoxic confusion may occur after surgery, a cardiac infarct, gastrointestinal bleeding, or occlusion or stenosis of the carotid arteries[cite: 16]. Nutritional deficiencies may cause mental symptoms or may be a symptom of a mental disorder[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: How many U.S. states have laws making it mandatory to report suspected elder abuse?
questions.explanation: At this time, 45 U.S. states have mandatory reporting laws for elder abuse[cite: 16]. Varying laws require specific professionals who have reason to suspect elder abuse or neglect to report their observations to designated public health agencies[cite: 16]. Criminal enforcement of these laws, which differ in nature from state to state, is nonexistent[cite: 16]. Clinical incentives to reporting, such as a having a comprehensive system of services to respond to such reports, providing appropriate follow-up services to victims and overstressed caregivers, and providing reporters with outcome of interventions, are lacking in most jurisdictions[cite: 16]. This situation and the relative isolation of most abused elderly persons from society have contributed to making mandatory reporting laws ineffective[cite: 16]. In addition, the fact that elder abuse statutes of the 1980s were based on child abuse laws of the 1960s makes the relevance of the elder abuse laws debatable, especially when ethical issues of beneficence, autonomy, and nonmaleficence are under consideration[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Visual hallucinations, delusions, fluctuating mental status, and adverse reactions to antipsychotic drugs, are all characteristics of which type of dementia?
questions.explanation:
Patients with Lewy body dementia may evidence visual hallucinations, delusions, fluctuating mental status, and adverse reactions to antipsychotic drugs[cite: 16].
Vascular dementia is estimated to account for 10 to 20 percent of the dementias of old age[cite: 16]. Classically, the disorder is characterized by a sudden onset of illness and stepwise decline in cognitive function rather than the insidious onset and gradually progressive course of Alzheimer’s disease[cite: 16].
Even though Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia constitute the bulk of all dementias, numerous other conditions must be considered and sometimes can be differentiated from Alzheimer’s disease by their clinical presentation[cite: 16]. For example, frontotemporal dementia is characterized by marked personality changes, relative preservation of visuospatial skills, and executive dysfunction[cite: 16]. Alcohol and drugs may cause memory loss and other symptoms of dementia[cite: 16]. For elderly patients, drugs deserve special emphasis as a cause of memory impairment because of widespread polypharmacy and age-related changes in body function and pharmacokinetics[cite: 16]. An elderly person’s brain can be extremely sensitive to change in its environment, and almost any physical illness can effect such a change and produce a dementia-like syndrome[cite: 16]. Numerous potentially treatable physical and mental conditions must be considered whenever the diagnosis of dementia is entertained
The clinical presentation of geriatric depression may mimic that of dementia[cite: 16]. The earlier term depressive pseudodementia is no longer considered useful because the dementia is real; instead, dementia syndrome of depression often is used[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Elderly persons taking antipsychotics are especially susceptible to the following side effects except
questions.explanation: Paresthesias, which are spontaneous tingling sensations, are not typically a side effect of antipsychotics[cite: 16]. Elderly persons, particularly if they have organic brain disease, are especially susceptible to the side effects of antipsychotics, which include dry mouth, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, and a toxic confusional state[cite: 16]. Tardive dyskinesia is characterized by disfiguring and involuntary buccal and lingual masticatory movements; akathisia is a restlessness marked by a compelling need for constant motion[cite: 16]. Choreiform body movements, which are spasmodic and involuntary movements of the limbs and the face, and rhythmic extension and flexion movements of the fingers may also be noticeable[cite: 16]. Examination of the patient’s protruded tongue for fine tremors and vermicular (worm-like) movements is a useful diagnostic procedure[cite: 16]. A toxic confusional state, also called a central anticholinergic syndrome, is characterized by a marked disturbance in short-term memory, impaired attention, disorientation, anxiety, visual and auditory hallucinations, increased psychotic thinking, and peripheral anticholinergic side effects[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Abnormalities of cognitive functioning in elderly persons are most often caused by
questions.explanation: Abnormalities of cognitive functioning in elderly adults are most often caused by some cerebral dysfunction or deterioration, although they may also be the result of depressive disturbances, schizophrenia, or the effects of medication[cite: 16]. In many instances, intellectual difficulties are not obvious, and a searching evaluation is necessary to detect them[cite: 16]. Elderly adults are sensitive to the effects of medication; in some instances, cognitive impairment may result from overmedication[cite: 16]. Hypochondriasis, the fear that one has a disease or preoccupation with one’s health, is not the cause of an abnormality of cognitive functioning[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Neuroimaging of brains in Alzheimer’s disease

options.text: reveals T2 hyperintensities on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
reveals reductions in the entorhinal cortex on volumetric MRI
reveals reductions in the cerebral metabolic rate for glucose (CMRgl)

questions.explanation: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies in Alzheimer’s disease show an increased number of T2 hyperintensities, as well as an increased number of hyperintensities in periventricular regions[cite: 16]. Positron emission tomography (PET) studies find abnormalities in the cerebral metabolic rate for glucose (CMRgl)[cite: 16]. Volumetric MRI studies find reductions in the volume of medial temporal lobe structures, namely the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, which are correlated with the severity of cognitive impairment, and increased rates of atrophy in medial temporal structures and the whole brain in patients with Alzheimer’s disease[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true?

options.text: The prevalence of major depression is higher in elderly than in younger patients.
In general, elderly African Americans are less distressed than elderly whites.
Aging results in a decreased ability to inhibit negative emotions.
Older adults experience sadness more than younger people.

correct_answer.text: In general, elderly African Americans are less distressed than elderly whites.

correct_answers.text: In general, elderly African Americans are less distressed than elderly whites.

questions.explanation:
Interesting racial differences have been noted between elderly African American and white people when measuring psychological distress[cite: 16]. Elderly African Americans have been noted to be less distressed than elderly whites[cite: 16]. It has been suggested that elderly African Americans may be afforded higher status and stay more engaged within their communities than elderly whites[cite: 16].
With the exception of dementing disorders and delirium, mental disorders are no more common in elderly people than in younger age groups[cite: 16]. Prevalence estimates of common disorders such as major depression are lower for those older than the age of 65 years than they are in younger cohorts[cite: 16]. Older adults report experiencing less negative emotions such as sadness, anger, and fear than younger adults, and aging is associated with an increased ability to inhibit negative emotional states and maintain positive emotional states[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the pharmacological treatment of the elderly is false?

options.text: Elderly persons use more medications than any other age group.
About 25 percent of prescriptions are for those older than age 65 years.
In the United States, 250,000 people a year are hospitalized because of adverse reactions to medications.
About 25 percent of hypnotics dispensed in the United States each year are to those older than age 65 years.
About 70 percent of elderly adults use over-the-counter medications.

correct_answer.text: About 25 percent of hypnotics dispensed in the United States each year are to those older than age 65 years.

correct_answers.text: About 25 percent of hypnotics dispensed in the United States each year are to those older than age 65 years.

questions.explanation: Psychotropic drugs are among those most commonly prescribed for elderly patients; 40 percent (not 25 percent) of all hypnotics dispensed in the United States each year are to those older than age 65 years[cite: 16]. Elderly patients use more medications than any other age group[cite: 16]. Indeed, 25 percent of all prescriptions are written for those older than age 65 years[cite: 16]. Many old persons have adverse drug reactions, as evidenced by the fact that, in the United States, 250,000 people a year are hospitalized because of adverse medication reactions[cite: 16]. Physicians must remember that about 70 percent of elderly people use over-the-counter (OTC) medications[cite: 16]. These preparations can interact with prescribed drugs and lead to dangerous side effects[cite: 16]. Physicians should include the use of OTC medications when taking a patient’s drug history[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: All of the following risk factors for dementia of the Alzheimer’s type are regarded as confirmed except
questions.explanation:
The power of individual case-control studies of dementia of the Alzheimer’s type has been greatly enhanced by an initiative undertaken by the European Consortium on Dementia (EURODEM) established by the European community[cite: 16]. The EURODEM carried out a collaborative reanalysis of 11 case-controlled studies, six from the United States and one each from Australia, Finland, Italy, Japan, and the Netherlands[cite: 16]. That analysis revealed risk factors that had hitherto been only speculative[cite: 16]. From this and other sources, only four risk factors can now be regarded as confirmed[cite: 16].
As for dementia in general, the incidence rises steeply with age, making it the strongest of all risk factors[cite: 16]. Having a parent or sibling with dementia of the Alzheimer’s type increases the risk of developing the disease about 3.5 times[cite: 16]. The risk is greater for relatives of early-onset patients than later-onset patients[cite: 16]. In interpreting the epidemiological data for individual patients, however, the clinician needs to emphasize that the risk conferred by a positive family history depends on how long that person lives[cite: 16]. Those who do not reach old age have a low risk[cite: 16]. Even for relatives who live to age 90 years, the probability that they themselves will develop the disease is only about 50 percent[cite: 16].
The much rarer, early-onset dementia of the Alzheimer’s type is caused by single genes, such as a mutation of the amyloid precursor gene on chromosome 21 or the presenilin genes on chromosomes 1 and 14[cite: 16]. But in most cases of dementia of the Alzheimer’s type, onset is not until the 70s or 80s[cite: 16]. In this group, of much greater public health importance, there are multiple genetic and environmental influences[cite: 16]. One of the most exciting discoveries is that the apolipoprotein E ε4 allele on chromosome 19 affects the risk of developing the disease[cite: 16]. The ε4 allele of this gene increases risk; the ε2 allele may reduce it[cite: 16]. Although early research with clinical samples showed a very strong relationship between apolipoprotein E ε4 genotype and dementia of the Alzheimer’s type, more recent studies with general population samples show a weaker relationship[cite: 16]. It is now clear that although all individuals with the ε4 allele are at increased risk, even homozygotes can live to age 90 years with only a 50 percent chance of developing dementia[cite: 16]. An interesting proposal is that the apolipoprotein E genotype predicts when (not whether) a person is predisposed to develop this dementia[cite: 16]. These epidemiological findings may in time lead to the development of pharmacological methods to slow the deposition of β-amyloid[cite: 16].
Persons with Down syndrome may develop the brain changes of dementia of the Alzheimer’s type before age 40 years[cite: 16]. This is believed to be related to their having an extra copy of the amyloid precursor gene on chromosome 21[cite: 16].
Because aluminum, known to be neurotoxic, occurs in neuritic plaques, evidence has been sought for an association between exposure to this metal and the development of dementia of the Alzheimer’s type[cite: 16]. Aluminum is ingested in food, drinking water, antacids, and toothpaste[cite: 16]. It is used in kitchen utensils and is applied to the body in antiperspirants[cite: 16]. The widespread use of aluminum as a flocculent in water supplies has led to public concern, although drinking water provides only a tiny percentage of dietary aluminum[cite: 16]. The amount absorbed depends on its bioavailability, and considerable uncertainty exists about its subsequent deposition in the brain[cite: 16]. From the epidemiological evidence, involvement of aluminum from drinking water or other sources in causing dementia of the Alzheimer’s type remains unproven[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Possible protective factors against dementia include
questions.explanation:
A recurrent finding in field surveys is that rates for dementia and cognitive impairment are higher in elderly persons who have had little education[cite: 16]. This may be partly attributable to bias in ascertainment, whereby the tests are done better by persons who are more literate[cite: 16]. Although such bias may be present in the detection of mild impairment in surveys, it is much less likely to influence the diagnosis of a fully developed dementia[cite: 16]. One interpretation is that education may delay the point at which a developing dementia becomes clinically manifest[cite: 16]. A longitudinal study of American nuns suggests that education and intelligence may actually protect against the neuropathological processes in dementia of the Alzheimer’s type[cite: 16]. This means that exposure to education in childhood may conceivably have some protective effect many decades later[cite: 16].
Because an inverse association between rheumatoid arthritis and dementia of the Alzheimer’s type was first observed, more than 20 publications have examined the possibility that persons who have taken steroids, aspirin, or other nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs over long periods have a lower risk of dementia or have slower cognitive decline in late life[cite: 16]. The most recent information is that antiinflammatory drugs probably do prevent or attenuate the symptoms of dementia of the Alzheimer’s type[cite: 16]. This effect is biologically plausible in terms of the action of these drugs to inhibit the immune and chronic inflammatory pathology suspected to apply in dementia of the Alzheimer’s type[cite: 16]. But it is premature for physicians to prescribe antiinflammatory drugs for dementia of the Alzheimer’s type before their effect is established in a randomized controlled trial and the findings balanced with their risks[cite: 16].
Case-controlled studies suggest possible protection against dementia of the Alzheimer’s type afforded to women who take estrogen[cite: 16]. But because these women also tend to be better educated and to differ in other lifestyle factors, this finding could be misleading[cite: 16]. The use of estrogen replacement therapy is currently controversial[cite: 16].
A large population-based prospective study in Bordeaux, France, has found evidence that moderate consumption of red wine protects against the onset of dementia[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors is common in victims of elder abuse?
questions.explanation: A shared living situation, social isolation, and dementia are risk factors that are commonly shared by victims of elder abuse[cite: 16]. Risk factors that may be common to abusers include mental illness, hostility, and alcohol or drug abuse[cite: 16]. Table 55.1 illustrates some characteristics associated with victimization and perpetration of elder mistreatment[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: An 85 year old woman with acute dementia sits on the sofa as her children discuss her medical and financial business. Her son suggests that this discussion should be continued at a later time, away from his mother’s presence because he fears upsetting her. To this, her daughter responds by saying “What does it matter, she doesn’t understand us anyway? She was always dumb to begin with, but now she’s really clueless.” As the woman looks on, her son shrugs “I guess you’re right. She doesn’t know what we are saying,” and their conversation continues without further interruption. The woman is a victim of which type of abuse?
questions.explanation: The woman is a victim of psychological abuse[cite: 16]. Subtypes of elder mistreatment include the following: (1) psychological abuse: conduct inflicting emotional distress or psychological harm; (2) physical abuse: physical acts causing pain or injury; (3) sexual assault: nonconsensual sexual contact of any kind; (4) financial exploitation: illegal taking, misuse, or concealment of funds, property, or assets of a vulnerable elderly person; and (5) neglect: committed by a person responsible for the vulnerable older adult[cite: 16].

questions.question_text: According to Holly Ramsey Klawsnik, all of the following are typologies of perpetrators of elder abuse characterized by personal gain, except
questions.explanation:
Holly Ramsey-Klawsnik identified five types of perpetrators of elder abuse: impaired, overwhelmed, narcissistic, domineering or bullying, and sadistic[cite: 16]. Impaired perpetrators are caregivers who mean to provide good care for their elderly loved ones but are unable to adequately care for the older adults in their care because of their own deficits[cite: 16]. Examples include caregivers who have physical or mental illness and are unaware of their limitations[cite: 16]. The overwhelmed perpetrators are similarly well meaning but become frustrated and lash out at the older adults in their care[cite: 16]. This was the most common perception of early elder abuse research, and preventive interventions were aimed at reducing caregiver stress[cite: 16]. Later research has shown, however, that caregiver stress is a much less common cause of mistreatment toward older adults[cite: 16]. Instead, recent studies indicate that the frustration associated with caregiver stress becomes directed inward toward the caregivers, and the caregivers’ health suffers[cite: 16].
Narcissistic, domineering or bullying, and sadistic perpetrators share the characteristic of personal gain[cite: 16]. Narcissistic perpetrators put their personal needs ahead of those of the victims[cite: 16]. Secondary gain, often financial, is their only goal[cite: 16]. Domineering or bullying perpetrators believe that their maltreatment of elderly individuals is justified[cite: 16]. Control of older adults is rationalized, and often ageism and the belief that older adults are weak and undeserving of respect contribute to the justification and continued victimization[cite: 16]. Sadistic perpetrators are the most brutal type[cite: 16]. These perpetrators lack remorse and derive pleasure from making others experience pain[cite: 16]. Older adults are intimidated, tormented, and terrorized to please the perpetrator[cite: 16].
